No. 7· 14 September 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. OpenAI's ChatGPT Ads go mainstream on both sides of the Atlantic the same day, 10 September: Amazon Ads pilots a US extension with Delta Vacations as first advertiser, Adform becomes the technology partner for the European rollout with Volkswagen and Vodafone testing.

  2. An IAB survey of 211 US buyers finds 86% expect to change how they measure media performance within twelve months because of conversational AI, but only 16% can currently measure brand visibility inside AI platforms at all.

  3. Adidas apologizes within days after its Single Shoe campaign featuring disabled Israeli veteran Shalev Biton draws boycott calls, the same week a 156 year old Italian yacht maker puts itself through its first rebrand in years.

The world

ppc.land, ExchangeWire, Marketing Dive · 10 Sep 2026

ChatGPT Ads go live on both sides of the Atlantic

Amazon opened a US pilot letting select Amazon DSP advertisers extend campaigns into ChatGPT, with Delta Vacations as the first advertiser; ads appear as text or image units beneath the chatbot's answers, aimed at the consideration and decision stages of the customer journey. The same day, OpenAI named Adform a technology platform partner for the European rollout of ChatGPT Ads, giving Volkswagen and Vodafone a managed route to test the format and tie results back into their wider campaign measurement. ChatGPT advertising crossed a $1 billion annualized run rate by 1 September 2026, having launched at $60 CPM with a $200,000 to $250,000 minimum buy and fallen to about $25 CPM by mid April as more than 600 advertisers joined.

Why it mattersTwo of digital advertising's biggest distribution partners, Amazon's shopping data and Europe's largest ad tech vendor, plugged into the same conversational surface on the same day. The ad unit that used to sit beside search results is becoming a line inside the answer itself.
IAB, martech.org · 10 Sep 2026

Most ad buyers expect to change how they measure everything within a year

A survey of 211 US brand and agency ad investment decision makers, part of IAB's “2026 Outlook Study: September Update,” found 86% expect to change how they measure media performance within twelve months because of conversational AI tools, most commonly by adding measurement of brand visibility inside AI platforms. Only 16% currently have that capability in any systematic form; 45% struggle to compare AI-driven and traditional customer journeys, 35% cannot get consistent data on brand visibility and citations in AI tools, and 30% cite missing or unreliable AI referral data.

Why it mattersThe measurement infrastructure is running roughly a year behind the ad inventory. Buyers are being asked to spend into ChatGPT and similar surfaces before they have a reliable way to prove what that spend did.
Digiday, Madison & Wall · 10 Sep 2026

AI-directed ad spend nearly doubles its share of the US market

Madison & Wall's revised forecast puts AI-directed ad spend, meaning dollars flowing through automated or AI-managed campaign types, at 12% of the roughly $479 billion US ad market excluding political spending in 2026, up from 2% in 2023. By 2030 the firm expects that share to reach 27%, about $158 billion. “This is a share shift,” said Luke Stillman, managing director at Madison & Wall.

Why it mattersThis is the budget-line version of the IAB survey above. The dollars are already moving into AI-managed buying roughly six times faster than they were three years ago, well ahead of the measurement tools catching up to explain what that spend is doing.
JTA, Jerusalem Post · 8 Sep 2026

Adidas apologizes after a disabled-veteran ad draws boycott calls

Adidas ran a Hebrew-language promotion for its Single Shoe service, which sells individual shoes to amputees, featuring Shalev Biton, a former Israeli soldier who lost his leg in 2021. The ad did not mention his military service. Pro-Palestinian activists called for a boycott, citing the high number of amputees in Gaza since October 2023, and the video drew rapid, coordinated criticism online. Adidas apologized on Monday 8 September via its Adidas Arabia Instagram account, saying “it was never our intent to cause offence,” a response the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel called insufficient.

Why it mattersThe product feature itself was neutral, a shoe service for amputees. The messenger carried context the ad never addressed, and in a market this charged, silence on that point became the whole story.

Social trends

TikTok via Reels · Sep 2026

Right Round Hangover

  • TikTok's paparazzi-prank format lands on Reels: creators stage a full “Hangover”-movie aftermath scene, wreckage and chaos, around someone who's still asleep, then reveal it with a flash-photo jump scare.
  • Runs on a licensed Flo Rida track, creator accounts only under current licensing.
  • Status: hot this week, a direct crossover from a TikTok format that made the jump to Reels intact rather than getting reinvented for the platform.
Why it mattersA prank format that already worked on one platform is spreading to a second one unchanged, which says the joke is stronger than either platform's native conventions.
Instagram Reels · Sep 2026

“What did my husband pray for”

  • Opposites-attract bait and switch: creators open on their calm, composed partner explaining they prayed for someone patient and steady, then cut hard into a compilation of that same partner being completely unhinged.
  • Set to Taylor Swift's “The Fate of Ophelia,” which has pulled 1.2 million Reels on the format (newengen).
  • Status: currently viral, a clean example of a trend that only works because the caption promises one thing and the cut delivers the opposite.
Why it matters1.2 million Reels on one track is a real number, not a vibe. It confirms the couple-bait-and-switch structure still has room to run months after its first variants appeared.
TikTok · early Sep 2026

The ancestor photo prank

  • Creators send a parent or grandparent a black-and-white, sepia-toned portrait, an AI-aged selfie or a repurposed celebrity photo (Kim Kardashian's bow-blouse editorial shot is the most recycled one), and claim it's a great-great-great-grandparent found on Ancestry.com.
  • The joke sits entirely in how sincerely the relative accepts it before the reveal.
  • Status: one of TikTok's defining formats of early September, spreading fast because dedicated tools turn any selfie into an aged portrait in two taps, no editing skill required.
Why it mattersThe friction that used to slow a trend down, needing an edited image, is gone. When the tool does the hard part in two taps, the format spreads at the speed of the joke alone.

Reading: all three trends this cycle are built on a reveal the audience doesn't see coming, a sleeping friend, a chaotic partner, a fake ancestor. None of them work on a first watch either: they're designed to be described to someone else before that person hits play, which is a cheaper distribution mechanism than any hashtag challenge.

Campaigns & brand moves

Primaonline · 8 Sep 2026

Cranchi Yachts rebrands for the first time in years

Italian yacht maker Cranchi, founded in 1870 and still family-owned across six generations, debuted a full rebrand by agency Adverteam at the Cannes Yachting Festival (8 to 13 September). The new identity drops the “Boatbuilders since 1870” payoff from the logo, introduces a palette drawn from Lake Como sunrise colors, and organizes the boat range into three narrative worlds (Orizzonte, Aria, Marea) built around lifestyle intent rather than technical specification. The platform is called “A Journey That Never Ends,” positioning 156 years of history as an ongoing story instead of a static heritage claim.

Why it mattersMost heritage brands lean on their founding date as the whole argument. Cranchi is betting the opposite, that the date matters less than the fact the story never stopped, which lets a 156 year old company talk to a buyer who wants lifestyle, not provenance.
Food Affairs, Media Key · 24 Aug – 12 Sep 2026

Fiordifrutta makes fruit its own biggest competitor

For its 30th anniversary, Rigoni di Asiago's Fiordifrutta jam brand and agency AL.TA built a campaign on one line: “the greatest invention since fruit itself.” It opened by moving jars out of the jam aisle and into fresh produce sections and fruit shops in Milan, so the product sat among the crates it was arguing against. That teaser phase led into sampling and creator activations, then a TV spot directed by Davide Polato and a multi-subject out-of-home run with lines like “what's better than wild blueberry Fiordifrutta? Wild blueberries,” each shown immersed in the actual fruit.

Why it mattersInstead of competing on flavor or price against other jam brands, Fiordifrutta picked a competitor no jam can ever beat on paper, the raw ingredient, and turned “we lose that argument on purpose” into the whole campaign.

What is working in content

newengen trend tracking · Sep 2026

“Potential-maxxing” replaces vague affirmations with a number

The self-improvement genre's newest variant drops phrases like “unlocking my potential” in favor of a hard number on screen, post counts, follower growth, revenue, view totals, then a short voiceover explaining the habit behind it. Newengen's September trend tracking flags it as a rising format specifically because it swaps a claim for a receipt.

Why it mattersThe format is a small tell about where audience trust sits right now. A vague motivational line reads as content; a number on screen reads as evidence, even inside a genre built entirely on personal anecdote.
Zebracat data via short-form video roundups · 2026

The two-second hook keeps deciding everything

Aggregated 2026 short-form benchmarks put the viewer decision window at a few seconds: shorts with an immediate hook in the first two seconds retain 19% more viewers than a slow start, and 71% of viewers decide within the first few seconds whether to keep watching. This is compiled benchmark data from a video-editing tool vendor, not an independent industry study, and is flagged as such.

Why it mattersThe number moves year to year but the mechanism doesn't. Every trend in this brief's social section, the paparazzi-prank reveal, the chaotic-partner cut, the ancestor-photo prank, front-loads its punchline setup in the first beat for exactly this reason.

The historical bridge

Atlanta, 12 May 1914

The reading notice that looked like news

The Atlanta Constitution ran a full page for Oglethorpe Park, a new subdivision now part of Brookhaven, written exactly like a news story: headline, body copy, a reporter's voice describing the lots and the streetcar line reaching them, no visual break from the actual news around it. Only a small label, “advertisement,” in tiny type gave it away. These were called “reading notices” in the trade, common enough by the 1900s and 1910s that they provoked an industry fight. Printers' Ink, the advertising trade magazine, backed a 1911 model law making false and deceptive advertising a criminal misdemeanor; by 1929 it had passed in 23 states, and press associations separately began requiring the word “advertisement” on anything written to look like news.

Why it still holds. ChatGPT Ads placing sponsored content beneath the chatbot's response, inside the same trusted conversational flow a user just asked a real question in, is the 1914 reading notice with a language model instead of a reporter's byline. The 1911 fight was never about whether paid content could exist next to editorial content, it was about whether the reader could tell which was which. That is the same question the IAB's 86% and the ad platforms racing into ChatGPT are all going to have to answer again.
